[ae] The vowel sound in "mat" is made with your mouth
open not too wide and the sound comes from just in the
back of your mouth, not quite as far as your throat.
Pretend someone is choking you.
The sound you will make is this "mat" vowel.
[ei] This sound is what pronunciation experts call a
dipthong.
A diphthong is actually two vowel sounds that are
pronounced together: we start out with one sound and
end up with another.
Your mouth moves when you say these sounds, so you
can’t make this sound for very long.
In comparison, when we made the [ae] sound in the first
part of this lesson, we can make that sound for a long
time.
To make this sound, start with your mouth slightly open
and your tongue pressed flat on the bottom of your
mouth.
The sides of your mouth are a little tense.
As you say this sound, close your mouth to bring the
sides of your top teeth down on to the sides of your
tongue.
Don’t close your mouth all the way.
This is also called a ‘voiced’ sound, which means your
vocal chords in your throat vibrate when you say it.

Don’t be confused: the sound at the end of "string", "ng",
is just one sound even though “n” and “g” have quite
different sounds by themselves.
To make this sound, put your tongue up against the roof
of the back of your mouth, as if you are going to say /k/ or
/g/.
Now, make a sound using your voice.
This is "ng".
In English, the "ng" sound is only found at the end of
syllables.
It cannot start a word.
/dz/ We’ve dealt with this sound before, in Lesson 10.
It’s the second half of the sound found in the “j” of
“jeans”.

[ei] This sound is what pronunciation experts call a
dipthong.
A diphthong is actually two vowel sounds that are
pronounced together: we start out with one sound and
end up with another.
Your mouth moves when you say these sounds, so you
can’t make this sound for very long.
In comparison, when we made the [ae] sound in the first
part of lesson 1, we can make that sound for a long time.
To make this sound, start with your mouth slightly open
and your tongue pressed flat on the bottom of your
mouth.
The sides of your mouth are a little tense.
As you say this sound, close your mouth to bring the
sides of your top teeth down on to the sides of your
tongue.
Don’t close your mouth all the way.
This is also called a ‘voiced’ sound, which means your
vocal chords in your throat vibrate when you say it.

/i:/ In English, we give some syllables more stress than

That means that some syllables are louder, longer, and
clearer than others.
Syllables that are unstressed are shorter, softer, and less
clear.

English.
These are the "Schwa" sound and the "barred i" sound.
The "barred i" is like a really short /I/ sound as in “heed”.
However, it is not drawn out, it is a very short-lasting
sound
